Share SOC 2 and security docs link
Schedule benchmark run on their 2k token prompt set (provision Dedicated trial)
Follow-up call to review pilot results w/ engineering team - target next week
action_items: Maya Chen: Send cost model + example config matrix; due 2026-03-09
Liam O'Connor: Prep benchmark guide and suggested prompt batching configs; due 2026-03-08

summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization) to hit Sequoia Analytics' budget. Customer leaned toward Dedicated for predictable throughput but wants cost comparison to Hosted and self-hosted. Next step: run benchmarks and share detailed pricing scenarios.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private economics
transcript: [00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intro - I'm Maya from Redwood, this is Liam, our systems SE.
[00:12] Raj: Hi, Raj here. Samantha and Diego are on too. We're trying to understand the cost math — per token and ops levers, basically before we pick Hosted vs Dedicated.

[00:22] Maya: Great. High level, we'll cover our per-token hosted pricing, what changes with Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and the levers like batching, prefix/K V cache, and quantization that change unit cost.

[00:35] Samantha (CTO): We have a hard budget target — roughly $60k/month for inference across the team. Current infra is a mix of cloud GPUs and a small self-hosted cluster, but cost is spiky and ops heavy.
[00:48] Liam (SE): To set expectations, unit costs vary a lot by model size, sequence length, and batching. We'll show a few scenarios — small replies 128 tokens, long-form 2k tokens.

[01:05] Diego: Our main workload is long-ish summaries: 1.2k to 2k tokens, steady 200 qps during business hours, with burst to 1k qps occasionally. Latency SLO is 300ms for interactive parts, 2s for longer jobs.

[01:28] Maya: That's helpful. So two axes: cost per token and latency. Dedicated helps with predictable throughput and lower tail latency because you get reserved capacity and can tune batching aggressively.
[01:45] Raj: Can you quantify "lower" — like how much cheaper per token are we talking with Dedicated vs Hosted?

[01:55] Liam: Rough numbers — hosted per-token baseline for a medium LLM is X cents per token at small scale. With Dedicated and right batching you can get 20-40% reduction in per-token compute costs; with quantization and caching it can be 40-70% depending on accuracy tolerances.
[02:20] Samantha: X cents is vague — can you give an example with 1.5k tokens on average?

[02:28] Maya: Sure. Example scenario we discussed: hosted generation at our public rates — say 0.0006 USD per token for the model variant. For a 1.5k token request that's ~0.90 per call. If you move to Dedicated and can batch to effective batch sizes of 16 and enable KV/prefix cache for repeated contexts, that could drop to ~0.45-0.6 per call compute-equivalent. Then quantization to int8 may shave more but impacts latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
[03:02] Raj: That 0.0006 number — does that include overheads, like network and infra margin, or just model compute?

[03:10] Liam: It's the billed token unit cost for hosted which bundles compute, routing, and platform. For Dedicated pricing we provide committed seat or capacity pricing: base infra fee + much lower per-token billing because infra is reserved. We'll send the spreadsheet with exact line items.
[03:30] Diego: How do batching and caching interact? If we batch aggressively, latency goes up which might break our 300ms SLO.

[03:40] Maya: Right — smart batching in Redwood is workload-aware: you set latency SLOs and the runtime does continuous batching to meet the SLO. For very tight SLOs you get smaller effective batches, so less cost savings. For background jobs or async paths you can batch bigger and save a lot.
[03:58] Raj: Can prefix caching help with summaries? We often have repeated sections in prompts (company context) that could be cached.

[04:05] Liam: Absolutely. Prefix/K V cache stores key/value attention states for repeated prompt prefixes. If 40% of the tokens are repeated context, you avoid re-computing them and you save proportionally. In practice we see 15-45% token cost reduction depending on repetition.
[04:26] Samantha: Any gotchas on cache invalidation and memory usage? Our prompts change weekly.

[04:33] Liam: Cache TTLs are configurable. For Dedicated you can allocate larger KV memory. Also we support prefix hashing so when the prefix changes slightly you can still reuse parts, but it's noisy. We'll include suggested TTLs in the guide.
[04:50] Raj: What about quantization — you mentioned accuracy tradeoffs. We can't tolerate hallucinations increasing.

[04:58] Maya: Quantization (int8, int4) lowers GPU memory and can reduce cost by enabling higher packing density or faster kernels. Most customers use 8-bit for production; we run evals on your prompt set in the pilot to surface any quality regressions. We also support mixed-precision and model variants for fallbacks.
[05:18] Diego: For our 2k token job, do you recommend Hosted with caching or Dedicated?

[05:24] Liam: If budget's fixed and predictable throughput matters, Dedicated is usually better. Hosted is easier to start and good for bursty unpredictable traffic. There's also Private (VPC/on-prem) if you have strict data residency or air-gap needs, but that changes support and cost structure.
[05:40] Samantha: Security — we need SOC2, SSO via SAML, and our KMS integration. How does Redwood handle KMS?
[05:48] Maya: We support KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated; hosted supports customer-managed keys with some limitations. We'll share the SOC 2 pack and our security whitepaper link.
[05:58] Raj: Great. On billing, can you show the math for our expected 200 qps steady state?

[06:05] Liam: We'll model request distribution: 200 qps * average tokens * hours. For example 200 qps * 1,500 tokens * 3600 sec * 8 hours ~ 8.64B tokens per day incorrectly? wait, math — we should put sample table in the sheet. (brief laughter)
[06:28] Maya: To avoid confusion we'll compute tokens/hour: 200 qps * 3600 = 720k requests per hour? That's off. Let's re-calc in the sheet. We'll send a worked example with correct token totals.
[06:42] Samantha: Please do. Also we want to understand breakpoints where Dedicated becomes cheaper than Hosted given our committed spend.
[06:50] Maya: We'll include a break-even analysis: commit level vs expected per-token reductions. Typically at sustained millions of tokens/day Dedicated is attractive.
[07:05] Raj: On the Dedicated side, what's elasticity for bursts? We have mean 200 qps but spike to 1k qps sometimes.

[07:12] Liam: Dedicated supports burst capacity; there are policies for autoscale and burst credits. You can provision base capacity for steady-state and allow burst with pre-agreed overage pricing or with an autoscale buffer.
[07:28] Diego: If we do a pilot, can we test both Hosted and Dedicated on our prompt set?

[07:34] Maya: Yes. Typical pilot: run same workload against Hosted at our public API and a Dedicated trial cluster. We'll run benchmarks, measure per-token cost, latency percentiles, and document tradeoffs.
[07:45] Raj: Who sets up the Dedicated trial? How much involvement from our infra team?

[07:50] Liam: Redwood handles cluster provisioning and initial tuning; you'll have an SE-assisted onboarding where we connect to your VPC if Private, or set network rules for Dedicated. Minimal infra work from you unless it's Private.
[08:05] Samantha: Network egress costs — do you account for that?
[08:10] Maya: Egress is separate; in Dedicated we can colocate to reduce egress. We'll surface expected egress estimates in the sheet.
[08:20] Raj: Any specific models you'd recommend for our summaries? We currently evaluate opensource LLM-x and proprietary LLM-y.

[08:28] Liam: We have curated model catalog. For long-context summarization a mid-size encoder-decoder or decoder with attention optimizations works. We'll recommend variants and quantization-safe checkpoints; also run quality evals during pilot.
[08:45] Samantha: Can you walk me through an example pricing line item for Dedicated — base vs per-token?

[08:52] Maya: Example: Dedicated monthly commitment $40k for reserved GPUs + a lower per-token rate 0.00015 USD/token. So if you do 50M tokens that's 7.5k token cost + 40k base -> 47.5k total. For Hosted, that 50M tokens at 0.0006/token is 30k, so interestingly Hosted could be cheaper at this specific volume. The break-even depends on token volume and batch/caching gains.
[09:25] Raj: So Dedicated is only cheaper when you reach a threshold or leverage caching/quantization heavily.
[09:31] Maya: Exactly. We'll run the break-even curves for your volume and expected caching/batching efficiency. Also remember Dedicated reduces latency tail and operational burden.
[09:45] Diego: What about multitenant isolation? We have teams with separate projects and billing.
[09:50] Liam: Dedicated offers tenant routing and RBAC; we can configure per-team routes, quotas, and cost allocation tags.
[09:59] Samantha: For legal, we might need a DPA and SLA. Is that standard?
[10:05] Maya: Yes, enterprise contracts include DPA, SOC2 attestations, and we can negotiate SLAs for Dedicated customers. We'll loop legal once you request proposal.
[10:18] Raj: A few random questions — does Redwood support model version pinning and automatic rollback?
[10:24] Liam: Yes, model pinning, canaries, A/B rollouts, and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant if quality is within threshold.
[10:34] Maya: On the quality monitoring front, we can attach eval sets and run regression alerts tied to prompt sets so quantization or model updates don't regress your metrics.
[10:46] Samantha: Good. Diego will get us the prompt set after this call.
[10:50] Diego: I'll put together a ~200 prompt sample and the daily traffic shape. Expect an email later today.
[11:00] Raj: Let's talk about an example where caching yields little benefit — like highly unique prompts. How does that change the math?

[11:08] Liam: If prompts are fully unique you can't save much from caching; batching remains your main lever. If latency SLO prohibits large batches, cost savings are limited and Hosted might be better for occasional peaks.
[11:22] Maya: We'll include three scenarios: 1) high prefix reuse, 2) medium reuse, 3) no reuse. Each will have Hosted vs Dedicated ROI numbers.
[11:32] Samantha: What about pre-warming KV cache for scheduled jobs?
[11:37] Liam: You can pre-warm with a cold-to-warm policy; Dedicated helps because you can reserve memory and boot nodes faster.
[11:45] Diego: Any examples of customers who reduced unit cost by >50%?
[11:50] Maya: Yes — a couple with high prefix reuse and relaxed latency used Dedicated + int8 quant + large batching and saw >50% compute token reductions. We'll anonymize case studies in the doc.
[12:05] Raj: Okay next steps — the pilot timeline?

[12:10] Maya: Quick pilot could run 1-2 weeks: Day 1 integrate sample prompt set with Hosted to get baseline; Day 2-3 spin Dedicated trial and run same load; Day 4-7 run extended workloads and quality evals; Day 7-10 review and iterate.
[12:25] Samantha: Who will own billing for the pilot?
[12:29] Maya: Pilot is typically covered by Redwood credits for evaluation. If you want a dedicated reserved cluster, we'd prototype a short-term trial commit.
[12:40] Diego: We need to see p95 and p99 latencies — do you capture those out of the box?
[12:45] Liam: Yes, Redwood Console shows p50/p90/p95/p99, token-level cost and per-route breakdowns.
[12:55] Raj: One more — our legal team will want encryption at rest and in transit details.
[13:01] Maya: We'll send security docs including encryption, K M S integration notes, and SOC2 report.
[13:10] Samantha: Perfect. Anything else on pricing cliffs?
[13:14] Liam: There's sometimes a cliff when you move to a higher parallelism GPU; we document that in the spreadsheet — e.g., moving from 4-GPU to 8-GPU capacity changes unit economics.
[13:27] Raj: I noticed earlier you used the term "KV cache" but sometimes I've seen "K V cache" in notes; spelling doesn't matter but ensure we understand it's the same.
[13:36] Maya: Yep — same thing. We'll use consistent naming in the doc.
[13:42] Samantha: Ok let's recap aloud so we have alignment.

[13:47] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send detailed per-token pricing sheet, break-even analysis, security pack; Redwood SE to run benchmark guide and suggested batching configs; Sequoia to share prompt set and throughput targets; schedule follow-up to review pilot results. Does that sound right?
[14:05] Raj: Yes. Also please include example line items for egress and network.
[14:11] Maya: Will do.
[14:16] Diego: Any chance you can show a quick sample row for math during the call?
[14:20] Liam: We tried but it got messy — better in the sheet. We'll include multiple worked examples.
[14:28] Samantha: Timeline — can you get the sheet and SOC2 by Monday?
[14:33] Maya: Yes, we'll send the sheet and security docs by 2026-03-09. SE will prepare benchmark configs by 2026-03-08.
[14:42] Raj: Great. One small ask — include both Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private cost lines so legal can review options.
[14:49] Maya: We'll include all three and the break-even thresholds.
[14:55] Samantha: Thanks everyone, this was useful. Diego will send prompts and traffic shape.
[15:00] Diego: Sending today.
[15:05] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with the materials and schedule the benchmark kickoff. End of call.
[48:00] (call ended)
Notes: Transcription occasionally mislabels acronyms; some technical terms abbreviated. Speakers used both formal names and first names.
